title: The Relationship Between Feedback and Caring
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that people's response to criticism depends on whether they believe the leader cares about them. The post says recipients can tell whether feedback is meant to help, and that critique without perceived care is read as insulting and cynical. It adds that good intentions inside the leader are not enough; they must be made clear before extensive feedback is given. This is hardest with new relationships, strangers and long-term underperformers. The move is to establish caring first, so that resistance to feedback largely disappears and people actively seek it.
points: Recipients can tell whether a leader's criticism comes from caring or from judgment.
Critique without perceived intent to help is experienced as insulting, even when the leader does not mean it that way.
Feeling caring is insufficient; leaders must make their intentions visible before giving extensive feedback.
Establishing care is hardest with new relationships, strangers and chronic underperformers.
When caring comes first, people want the feedback and act on it, avoiding unnecessary resistance.
quotes: It is painfully obvious to those on the receiving end whether a leader cares about them as people and whether the intention of their criticism is to make them better.
People are suspicious of leaders who offer criticism without a clear motivation to help. They have the strong sense that evaluation and judgment without caring is cynical and scornful.
While leaders rarely do this on purpose, it is essential that they understand the importance of creating a context where their intentions are clear and the caring is palpable.
Even when this is the case, what they feel in their hearts and heads is not enough. They must make their intentions clear before offering extensive feedback.
Leaders who take the time to show others that they care about them and want to help them perform to reach their highest potential then find that people want their feedback and are ready to act on it.
In many cases, the aversion to critical feedback can easily be averted if leaders make the effort to create a foundation of caring and the desire to make others better.
